claims.text: Rapid thermal treatment limits atomic diffusion in the mixed-metal precursor.
Rapid heating causes the different metal species to nucleate nearly simultaneously.
Immediate quenching freezes atomic positions before diffusion can cause segregation or phase separation.
The rapid thermal process produces a homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The starting mixed-metal precursor is homogeneously impregnated and uniformly distributed on a high-surface-area support.
Gamma-alumina is a suitable granular support for supported high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
A rapid synthesis can be conducted at approximately 923 K.
The cited rapid treatment reaches approximately 923 K within seconds and is immediately quenched under inert atmosphere.
Conventional heating at 20 K/min takes about 31 minutes to rise from 298 K to 923 K and produces phase-segregated NiPdPt nanoparticles.
Prolonged atomic diffusion during slow heating causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Fast treatment yields more uniform elemental distributions and less phase segregation than slow treatment.
Fast treatment minimizes particle growth and yields smaller, well-dispersed nanoparticles relative to slow heating.
The smaller particles produced by fast treatment have higher surface-atom exposure.
Fast-treated particles may exhibit enhanced catalytic activity.
With limited free-atom mobility, random alloy formation becomes more likely as the number of atom types increases.
Five-element mixtures form a single phase more readily than binary mixtures under the studied conditions.
Single-phase binary alloys are restricted to systems exhibiting cooperative reduction under the studied conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not hold when strong precursor chemical coordination dominates reduction kinetics.
Changing only the thermal ramp rate should produce a marked improvement in phase homogeneity.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as varying only the heating ramp rate, but the ultrafast arm also explicitly includes immediate quenching while the slow arm's quench protocol is not specified. The design therefore couples ramp rate and quenching rather than clearly isolating one variable.

Enhanced catalytic activity is presented only as a potential secondary outcome, yet absence of a catalytic improvement is included as sufficient falsification. Catalytic performance can vary independently of whether the proposed homogeneous-alloy formation mechanism occurred.
